1.2 Short Repetition: Two-Sided \(t\)-Test






More Details: See our lecture on hypothesis testing for more details.



Statistical hypothesis:

\(\displaystyle H_0\colon \mu = 0\quad\) versus \(\displaystyle \quad H_1\colon \mu \neq 0\)


\(t\)-test statistic: \[
\mathrm{T} = \frac{\bar{X} - 0}{S/\sqrt{n}}\overset{H_0}{\sim} t_{n-1},
\] where

\(\bar{X}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\)
\(S= \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar{X})}\)

denote the empirical mean and the empirical standard deviation.






Assumptions:

Random (iid) sample: \(X_1,\dots,X_n\overset{\operatorname{iid}}{\sim}X\)
For small sample sizes: \(X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\)
For large sample sizes: \(\mathrm{E}(X)=\mu\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(X)=\sigma^2\)





Observed (obs) realization (marketing campaign):

\[
\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}} = \frac{\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}} - 0}{S_{\mathrm{obs}}/\sqrt{5}} = 0.84
\]

\(\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{i=1}^5 X_{i,obs} = 0.30\)
\(S_{\mathrm{obs}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{5-1}\sum_{i=1}^5(X_{i,obs}-\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}})} = 0.80\)

Critical Values: The critical values — the \((1-\alpha/2)\)- and the \(\alpha/2\)-quantiles of the \(t\)-distribution with \(\operatorname{df}=n-1\) — define the rejection regions for a given significance level \(0<\alpha<1\).

text:
1.3 \(\mathrm{p}\)-Values: Challenges for Hypothesis Testing
\(\mathrm{p}\)-values can be helpful tools, but they are often misused and misunderstood, leading to a large amount of published “bad science.”
This has sparked an ongoing debate about whether \(\mathrm{p}\)-values — and the idea of statistical significance — should be used at all


The problem with p Values: How significant are they, really? (Cumming 2013)


Scientific method: Statistical errors (Nuzzo 2014)


Scientists rise up against statistical significance (Amrhein, Greenland, and McShane 2019)


To address this, the American Statistical Association (ASA) released two statements explaining what \(\mathrm{p}\)-values and statistical significance can — and cannot — tell us.


The ASA statement on p-values: Context, process, and purpose (Wasserstein and Lazar 2016)


Moving to a world beyond “p< 0.05” (Wasserstein, Schirm, and Lazar 2019)



1.3.1 \(\mathrm{p}\)-Value Hacking: The Multiple Comparison Problem
\(\mathrm{p}\)-hacking happens when researchers keep adjusting their analysis until they find a statistically significant result \((\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} < \alpha)\) — even if there’s no real effect.
🧪 Typical tricks include:

Running lots of tests until one happens to be “significant.”
Changing the model setup (adding or removing variables) until an insignificant result turns “significant”.
Selectively including or excluding data points to turn an insignificant result turns “significant”.

This is called the multiple comparison problem — the more tests you run, the higher the chance of finding a false positive (falsely rejecting a correct \(H_0\)).

Multiple Comparison Problem






⚠️ Multiple Comparison Problem



 When multiple tests are conducted, the chance of finding at least one “significant” result purely by coincidence increases.
For instance, with \(m=20\) independent tests at the significance level \(\alpha = 0.05\), there is a \(64 \%\) chance of incorrectly rejecting at least one null hypothesis: \[\begin{align*}
& P(\text{rejecting at least one of the $m$ $H_0$'s}\mid \text{all }H_0\text{'s are true})\\[2ex]
=& 1-P(\text{not rejecting any of the $m$ $H_0$'s}\mid \text{all }H_0\text{'s are true})\\[2ex]
=& 1 - (1-\alpha)^m\\[2ex]
=& 1 - 0.95^{20} \;\approx \; 0.64
\end{align*}\]


Adjusting for Multiple Comparisons
The Bonferroni Correction requires using a more stringent significance threshold when multiple tests are performed; namely \[
\alpha_{\textrm{Bonf}}=\frac{\alpha}{m}
\] for \(m\) tests.
\[\begin{align*}
& P(\text{rejecting at least one of the $m$ $H_0$'s}\mid \text{all }H_0\text{'s are true})\\[2ex]
=& 1-P(\text{not rejecting any of the $m$ $H_0$'s}\mid \text{all }H_0\text{'s are true})\\[2ex]
=& 1 - (1-\alpha_{\textrm{Bonf}})^m\\[2ex]
=& 1 - \left(1-\frac{\alpha}{m}\right)^m\leq \alpha
\end{align*}\] For \(\alpha = 0.05\) and \(m=20\colon\) \[
1 - \left(1-\frac{0.05}{20}\right)^{20} = 0.0488
\]
Mitigating the Misuse of -Values


Pre-Registration: Researchers specify hypotheses and analytical methods before seeing the data, reducing the temptation to -hack.

The Open Science Framework
As Predicted



Replication: Independent replication studies help determine whether a result is robust or simply a random fluke (type I error).

Institute for Replication




1.3.2 Correct Interpretation of the \(\textrm{p}\)-Value
The \(\textrm{p}\)-value \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) measures how extreme \(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\) is if the null hypothesis \(H_0\) were true.







🤓 Small \(\textrm{p}\)-Values: \(\;\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} < \alpha\)






A small \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) suggests that the observed statistic \(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\) is inconsistent with the null hypothesis \(H_0\).
In that case, we may decide that \(H_0\) does not provide a plausible explanation for the data.
When we reject \(H_0\) (because \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} < \alpha\)), we accept a risk of making a type I error — that is, falsely rejecting a true \(H_0\) — with probability \(\alpha\).
This risk is typically considered acceptable for small significance levels such as \(\alpha = 0.05\) or \(\alpha = 0.01\).











⚠️ Large \(\textrm{p}\)-Values: \(\;\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} \geq \alpha\)






A large \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) means that the observed test statistic \(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\) is consistent with the null hypothesis \(H_0\).
❗️ However, this does not mean that \(H_0\) is true or confirmed.

Even very large \(\textrm{p}\)-values (e.g., \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} \approx 1\)) can occur simply because a given deviation from \(H_0\) does not stand out from the random variation captured by the standard error, for example when

the sample size \(n\) is small, or

the variability \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\) in the data is large.


When we fail to reject \(H_0\) (because \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} \geq \alpha\)), we cannot accept \(H_0\) as we don’t know the probability of making a type II error (falsely accepting \(H_0\)).


📢 Statistical tests are designed to reject \(H_0\) when there is enough evidence — not to prove that \(H_0\) is true.





1.3.3 General Don’t Do’s and Do’s






⚠️ Don’t Do’s






\(\mathrm{p}\)-values do not measure the probability that \(H_0\) is true.
\(\mathrm{p}\)-values do not measure the size of an effect or the importance of a result: Statistical significance does not (necessarily) mean practical significance.
Scientific conclusions and business or policy decisions should not be based only on whether a \(\mathrm{p}\)-value passes a specific \(\alpha\)-threshold.










🤓 Do’s







Be Thoughtful: Statistically thoughtful researchers …

recognize when they are doing exploratory studies (for generating statistical hypothesis) or more rigidly pre-planned studies (for testing statistical hypothesis).
prioritize sound data production by putting energy into the careful planning, design, and execution of the study.



Be Open:

Openness to transparency (share data, make results reproducible, etc.)
Openness in communication (statistical significance does not mean scientific importance, one study is rarely enough, etc.)



Be Modest:

There is no true statistical/econometric model.
Be modest about the role of statistical inference in scientific inference.




📢 Accept that there will always be uncertainty, and be thoughtful, open, and modest.

1.2 The Two-Sided \(\mathrm{p}\)-Value

1.2.1 Definition of the \(\mathrm{p}\)-Value






\(\mathrm{p}\)-Value: The \(\mathrm{p}\)-value, \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}},\) is the probability of observing a test statistic \(\mathrm{T}\) as extreme as or more extreme than \(\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) (in the direction(s) of the alternative hypothesis), given the null hypothesis (\(H_0\)) is true.


Two-Sided \(\mathrm{p}\)-Value: \[\displaystyle\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} = \mathrm{P}\big(\,|\mathrm{T}|\,\geq |\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\;\big|\;H_0\;\text{is true}\big)\]





The light-red area in Figure 1.3 equals the observed \(\mathrm{p}\)-value \(\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}=0.39\) corresponding to the observed value of the \(t\)-statistic \(\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}=0.96.\)







Figure 1.3: Density of the null-distribution \(t_{\operatorname{df}}\) with \(\operatorname{df}=n-1=4\) (marketing campaign data).





1.2.2 Computing the \(\mathrm{p}\)-Value
Note that \[
% \mathrm{T}=\frac{\bar{X}-0}{S/\sqrt{n}}\overset{H_0}{\sim}t_{n-1}
\mathrm{T}=\frac{\bar{X}-0}{S/\sqrt{n}}\overset{H_0}{\sim}t_{n-1}
\] implies that the absolute value \(|T|\) of the random \(t\)-statistic is Half-\(t_{n-1}\) distributed, \[
% \mathrm{T}=\frac{\bar{X}-0}{S/\sqrt{n}}\overset{H_0}{\sim}t_{n-1}
|\mathrm{T}|=\frac{|\bar{X}-0|}{S/\sqrt{n}}\overset{H_0}{\sim}\textrm{Half-}t_{n-1}.
\]
Figure 1.4 visualizes the density function of the \(\textrm{Half-}t_{n-1}\) distribution with \(n-1=4\) degrees of freedom for the marketing campaign data (\(n=5\)).







Figure 1.4: Densities of the null-distributions \(t_{\operatorname{df}}\) and \(\textrm{Half-}t_{\operatorname{df}}\) with \(\operatorname{df}=n-1=4\) (marketing campaign data).





The cumulative distribution function (cdf) of the Half-\(t\) distribution allows us to compute the \(\mathrm{p}\)-value of the two-sided \(t\)-statistic:
\[\begin{align*}
\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}
& = \mathrm{P}\big(\,|\mathrm{T}|\,\geq |\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\;\big|\;H_0\;\text{is true}\big)\\[1ex]
& = 1 - \mathrm{P}\big(\highlight{|\mathrm{T}|}\leq |\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\;\big|\highlight{H_0\;\text{is true}}\big)\\[1ex]
& = 1 - \highlight{\mathrm{F}_{\,\text{Half-}t,n-1}}\big(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\big),
\end{align*}\] where \(\mathrm{F}_{\,\text{Half-}t,n-1}\) denotes the cdf of the Half-\(t\) distribution with \(\operatorname{df}=n-1\)
Observed \(\mathrm{p}\)-Value (Marketing Campaign Data):
Since \(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|=0.96,\) \[
\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}=0.39=1 - \mathrm{F}_{\,\text{Half-}t,n-1}\big(0.96\big).
\]

1.2.3 Test Decision based on the \(\mathrm{p}\)-Value

We reject \(H_0\) and accept \(H_1\) at the significance level \(0<\alpha<1\) if \[
\highlight{\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} < \alpha}
\]
We fail to reject \(H_0\) at the significance level \(0<\alpha<1\) if \[
\highlight{\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} \geq \alpha}
\]

Test Decision (Marketing Campaign Data):
Since \[
\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}=0.39 \geq \alpha = 0.05
\] we fail to reject \(H_0\colon \mu =0\) at the significance level \(\alpha=0.05.\)
That is, we have no statistical evidence that the marketing campaign showed a tendency toward significantly higher or lower sales.






⚠️ Failing to reject \(H_0\) does not mean that \(H_0\) is true. It only means that a potential impact of the campaign is not large enough such that the observed effect \((\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}}-0)\) was not large enough to stand out from the random variation captured by the standard error \((S_{\mathrm{obs}}/\sqrt{n});\) see Section 1.2.5.





1.2.4 Equivalent Test Decisions using Critical Values and \(\mathrm{p}\)-Values
For a given significance level \(0<\alpha<1\), critical values and \(\mathrm{p}\)-values yield equivalent test decisions:

Reject \(H_0\)

if \(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}| > \mathrm{q}_{1-\alpha}\quad\) or
if \(\,\,\,\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\,<\alpha\)



Fail to reject \(H_0\)

if \(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}| \leq  \mathrm{q}_{1-\alpha}\quad\) or
if \(\,\,\,\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\, \leq \alpha\)




where \(\mathrm{q}_{1-\alpha}\) denotes the \((1-\alpha)\)-quantile of the Half-\(t_{n-1}\) distribution.


Reject \(H_0\)
Fail to Reject \(H_0\)

























1.2.5 Interpretation of the \(\textrm{p}\)-Value
By its definition, \(\textrm{p}\)-value \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) tells us the probability of observing a value of \(|\mathrm{T}|\) as extreme as or more extreme than \(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\) if the null hypothesis were \(H_0\).
That is, \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) measures how extreme \(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\) is if the null hypothesis \(H_0\) were true.






🤓 Small \(\textrm{p}\)-Values




A very small \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) suggests that \(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\) is incompatible with \(H_0\), so we may decide that \(H_0\) does not provide a plausible explanation for the data.
If we reject \(H_0\), since \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}<\alpha,\) we falsely reject \(H_0\) (type-I-error) with probability \(\alpha,\) which we may find acceptable for small \(\alpha\)-levels such as \(\alpha=0.05\) or \(\alpha = 0.01.\)










😑 Large \(\textrm{p}\)-Values



A large \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) suggests that \(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\) is compatible with \(H_0\), but this does not allow us to conclude that \(H_0\) is confirmed— even if \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\approx 1\).

Even when \(H_0\) is false, we may see very large values of \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) if, for instance,

the sample size \(n\) is small or

the variability \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\) in the data is large.


If we fail to reject \(H_0\), since \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\geq \alpha,\) we cannot simply accept \(H_0\), since we do not know at which probability we falsely accept \(H_0\) (type-II-error).



📢 Statistical hypothesis tests are designed to falsify \(H_0\) not to verify \(H_0.\)

More Details: See our lecture on hypothesis testing for more details.



Two-Sided \(t\)-Test
Statistical hypothesis:

\(\displaystyle H_0\colon \mu = 0\quad\) versus \(\displaystyle \quad H_1\colon \mu \neq 0\)


\(t\)-test statistic: \[
\mathrm{T} = \frac{\bar{X} - 0}{S/\sqrt{n}}\overset{H_0}{\sim} t_{n-1},
\] where

\(\bar{X}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\)
\(S= \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar{X})}\)

denote the empirical mean and the empirical standard deviation.






Assumptions:

Random (iid) sample: \(X_1,\dots,X_n\overset{\operatorname{iid}}{\sim}X\)
For small sample sizes: \(X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\)
For large sample sizes: \(\mathrm{E}(X)=\mu\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(X)=\sigma^2\)





Observed (obs) realization (marketing campaign):

\[
\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}} = \frac{\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}} - 0}{S_{\mathrm{obs}}/\sqrt{5}} = 0.84
\]

\(\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{i=1}^5 X_{i,obs} = 0.30\)
\(S_{\mathrm{obs}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{5-1}\sum_{i=1}^5(X_{i,obs}-\bar{X}_{\mathrm{obs}})} = 0.80\)
Critical Values






Critical Values: The critical values (the \((1-\alpha/2)\)- and the \(\alpha/2\)-quantiles of the \(t\)-distribution with \(\operatorname{df}=n-1\)) define the rejection regions for a given significance level \(0<\alpha<1\).



Figure 1.2 shows the density function of the \(t_{\operatorname{df}}\) distribution with \(\operatorname{df}=n-1=4;\) i.e., the null-distribution for our marketing campaign example.







Figure 1.2: Density function of the \(t_{\operatorname{df}}\) distribution with \(\operatorname{df}=n-1=4\) and the \((1-\alpha/2)\)- and the \(\alpha/2\)-quantile.




The observed value of the \(t\)-statistic \(\textrm{T}_{\textrm{obs}}=0.84\) not in one of the rejection regions of the two-sided \(t\)-test (Figure 1.2). Thus, we fail to reject the null-hypothesis \(H_0\colon\mu = 0\).

We’ll explore these questions using the two-sided \(t\)-test as our main example. Parallel arguments apply to one-sided testing and other hypothesis tests (F-test, etc.)

We want to know:

Research question:  Was the marketing campaign successful? Did it show a tendency (location-shift) toward significantly higher or lower sales?
Statistical question:  Is the mean, \(\mu,\) of \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) different from zero?

\mathrm{T} = \frac{\bar{X} - 0}{S/\sqrt{n}}\overset{H_0}{\sim} t_{n-1},
\] where

1.3 Equivalent Test Decisions using Critical Values and \(\mathrm{p}\)-Values
For a given significance level \(0<\alpha<1\), critical values and \(\mathrm{p}\)-values yield equivalent test decisions:

Reject \(H_0\)

if \(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}| > \mathrm{q}_{1-\alpha}\quad\) or
if \(\,\,\,\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\,<\alpha\)



Fail to reject \(H_0\)

if \(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}| \leq  \mathrm{q}_{1-\alpha}\quad\) or
if \(\,\,\,\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\, \leq \alpha\)




where \(\mathrm{q}_{1-\alpha}\) denotes the \((1-\alpha)\)-quantile of the Half-\(t_{n-1}\) distribution.


Reject \(H_0\)
Fail to Reject \(H_0\)

























1.3.1 Interpretation of the \(\textrm{p}\)-Value
By its definition, \(\textrm{p}\)-value \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) tells us the probability of observing a value of \(|\mathrm{T}|\) as extreme as or more extreme than \(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\) if the null hypothesis were \(H_0\).
That is, \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) measures how extreme \(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\) is if the null hypothesis \(H_0\) were true.






🤓 Small \(\textrm{p}\)-Values




A very small \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) suggests that \(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\) is incompatible with \(H_0\), so we may decide that \(H_0\) does not provide a plausible explanation for the data.
If we reject \(H_0\), since \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}<\alpha,\) we falsely reject \(H_0\) (type-I-error) with probability \(\alpha,\) which we may find acceptable for small \(\alpha\)-levels such as \(\alpha=0.05\) or \(\alpha = 0.01.\)










😑 Large \(\textrm{p}\)-Values



A large \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) suggests that \(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\) is compatible with \(H_0\), but this does not allow us to conclude that \(H_0\) is confirmed— even if \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\approx 1\).

Even when \(H_0\) is false, we may see very large values of \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) if, for instance,

the sample size \(n\) is small or

the variability \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\) in the data is large.


If we fail to reject \(H_0\), since \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\geq \alpha,\) we cannot simply accept \(H_0\), since we do not know at which probability we falsely accept \(H_0\) (type-II-error).



📢 Statistical hypothesis tests are designed to falsify \(H_0\) not to verify \(H_0.\)

Definition

Definition of the \(\mathrm{p}\)-Value



The \(\mathrm{p}\)-value, \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}},\) is the probability of obtaining a test statistic \(\mathrm{T}\) at least as extreme (in the direction(s) of the alternative hypothesis) as the one observed \((\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}})\) — assuming that \(H_0\) is true.


Two-sided \(\mathrm{p}\)-value of the \(t\)-test \[\displaystyle\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} = \mathrm{P}\big(\,|\mathrm{T}|\,\geq |\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\;\big|\;H_0\;\text{is true}\big)\]


The light-red area in Figure 1.2 equals the observed \(\mathrm{p}\)-value \(\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}=0.39\) corresponding to the observed value of the \(t\)-statistic \(\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}=0.96.\)







Figure 1.2: Density of the null-distribution \(t_{\operatorname{df}}\) with \(\operatorname{df}=n-1=4\) (marketing example).







🧮 Computing the \(\mathrm{p}\)-Value


Null Distribution
Density Function
Distribution Function



Note that \[
\mathrm{T}=\frac{\bar{X}-0}{S/\sqrt{n}}\overset{H_0}{\sim}t_{n-1}\phantom{Half}
\] implies that  \[
\highlight{|\mathrm{T}|}=\frac{|\bar{X}-0|}{S/\sqrt{n}}\overset{H_0}{\sim}\highlight{\textrm{Half-}t_{n-1}.}
\]










Figure 1.3: The density function of the Half-\(t_{n-1}\) distribution is the folded version of the density function of the \(t_{n-1}\) distribution.






\[\begin{align*}
\mathrm{F}_{\,\text{Half-}t_{n-1}}(x)&=\mathrm{P}(|\textrm{T}|\leq x\mid H_0\;\text{is true}),\quad |\textrm{T}|\overset{H_0}{\sim} \textrm{Half-}t_{n-1}
\end{align*}\]

\(\mathrm{F}_{\,\text{Half-}t_{n-1}}(x) =\) extraDistr::pht(q = x, nu = n - 1)








Figure 1.4: Distribution function of the null-distribution \(\textrm{Half-}t_{\operatorname{df}}\) with \(\operatorname{df}=n-1=4\) (marketing example).













Computing the \(\mathrm{p}\)-Value of the Two-Sided \(t\)-Test



 The distribution function \(\mathrm{F}_{\,\text{Half-}t_{n-1}}(x)\) of the Half-\(t\) distribution allows us to compute the \(\mathrm{p}\)-value, \(\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}},\) for the two-sided \(t\)-statistic \(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\):
\[\begin{align*}
\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}
& = \mathrm{P}\big(\,|\mathrm{T}|\,\geq |\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\;\big|\;H_0\;\text{is true}\big)\\[1ex]
& = 1 - \mathrm{P}\big(\highlight{|\mathrm{T}|}\leq |\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\;\big|\highlight{H_0\;\text{is true}}\big)\\[1ex]
& = 1 - \highlight{\mathrm{F}_{\,\text{Half-}t,n-1}}\big(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\big)
\end{align*}\]



Computing the \(\mathrm{p}\)-Value (Marketing Example)
\[\begin{align*}
\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}
&=1 - \mathrm{F}_{\,\text{Half-}t,n-1}\big(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\big)\\
&=1 - \mathrm{F}_{\,\text{Half-}t,n-1}\big(\,0.96\,\big)=0.39
\end{align*}\]


Plot
R-Codes



Computation of the observed \(\operatorname{p}\)-value:










Computation of the observed \(\operatorname{p}\)-value:

library("extraDistr")
n  <- 5
df <- n - 1

## 1 minus the distribution function of the Half-t
p_obs <- 1 - pht(q = abs(T_obs), nu = df)

## Alternatively: 
result <- t.test(X_obs, mu = 0, alternative = "two.sided")
p_obs  <- result$p.value




⚖️ Test Decision based on the \(\mathrm{p}\)-Value


We reject \(H_0\) at the significance level \(0<\alpha<1\) if \[
\highlight{\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} < \alpha}
\]
We fail to reject \(H_0\) at the significance level \(0<\alpha<1\) if \[
\highlight{\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} \geq \alpha}
\]


Test Decision (Marketing Example)
Since \[
\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}=0.39 \geq \alpha = 0.05
\] we fail to reject \(H_0\colon \mu =0\) at the significance level \(\alpha=0.05.\)







⚠️ Failing to reject \(H_0\) does not mean that \(H_0\) is true.





 Failing to reject \(H_0\) only means that a potential impact of the marketing campaign is not large enough to stand out from the random variation captured by the standard error \((S_{\mathrm{obs}}/\sqrt{n});\) see ?sec-MissUses.

“Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.” (Sagan 1997).

## \(\mathrm{p}\)-Values: Misused and Misunderstood {#sec-MissUses}



\(\mathrm{p}\)-values can be powerful tools — when used correctly. But in practice, they’re often misused and misinterpreted, leading to a surprising amount of published “bad science.”



This misuse has sparked an ongoing debate: Should we rely on \(\mathrm{p}\)-values and the concept of statistical significance at all?


📚 Further reading:



* The problem with p Values: How significant are they, really? (Cumming 2013) * Scientific method: Statistical errors (Nuzzo 2014) * Scientists rise up against statistical significance (Amrhein, Greenland, and McShane 2019)



To clarify what \(\mathrm{p}\)-values and statistical significance actually mean (and what they don’t), the American Statistical Association (ASA) published two landmark position papers:


📄 ASA Statements:



* The ASA statement on p-values: Context, process, and purpose (Wasserstein and Lazar 2016) * Moving to a world beyond “p< 0.05” (Wasserstein, Schirm, and Lazar 2019)



<!– ### 🧭 What \(\mathrm{p}\)-Values Tell Us — and What They Don’t {-}


::: {.callout-tip appearance=“minimal”} ## ✅ What \(\mathrm{p}\)-values do tell us 



* They measure how compatible the data (i.e., the test statistic) are with the null hypothesis \(H_0\).


* A small \(\mathrm{p}\)-value means the observed data (i.e., the test statistic) would be unlikely if \(H_0\) were true.


:::


::: {.callout-caution appearance=“minimal”}


## 🚫 What \(\mathrm{p}\)-values do not tell us 



* They do not give the probability that \(H_0\) is true or false.


* They do not tell us whether a result is practically important. ::: –>


### 🙁 \(\mathrm{p}\)-Hacking {-}



\(\mathrm{p}\)-hacking is arguably the most common misuse of \(\mathrm{p}\)-values. It happens when researchers keep adjusting their analysis until they find a statistically significant result \((\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} < \alpha)\) — even if there’s no real effect.


🧪 Typical “tricks” include:


* Running lots of tests until one happens to be “significant.”


* Changing the model setup (adding or removing variables) until an insignificant result turns “significant”.


* Selectively including or excluding data points to turn an insignificant result into a “significant” one.


This is called the multiple comparison problem — the more tests you run, the higher the chance of finding a false positive (falsely rejecting a correct \(H_0\)).

Multiple Comparison Problem


Source: https://xkcd.com/882/







⚠️ Multiple Comparison Problem



 When multiple tests are conducted, the chance of finding at least one “significant” result purely by coincidence increases.
For instance, with \(m=20\) independent tests at the significance level \(\alpha = 0.05\), there is a \(64 \%\) chance of incorrectly rejecting at least one null hypothesis: \[\begin{align*}
& P(\text{rejecting $H_0$ in at least one of the $m$ tests}\mid \text{all }H_0\text{'s are true})\\[2ex]
=& 1-P(\text{not rejecting $H_0$ in each of the $m$ tests}\mid \text{all }H_0\text{'s are true})\\[2ex]
=& 1-\left(P(\text{not rejecting $H_0$ in one single test}\mid H_0 \text{ is true})\right)^m\\[2ex]
=& 1-\left(1-P(\text{rejecting $H_0$ in one single test}\mid H_0 \text{ is true})\right)^m\\[2ex]
=& 1-\left(1-P(\text{type I error})\right)^m\\[2ex]
=& 1 - (1-\alpha)^m\\[2ex]
=& 1 - 0.95^{20} \;\approx \; 0.64
\end{align*}\]


Adjusting for Multiple Comparisons






🤓 The Bonferroni Correction



 The Bonferroni Correction requires using a more stringent significance threshold when multiple tests are performed; namely \[
\alpha_{\textrm{Bonf}}=\frac{\alpha}{m}
\] for \(m\) tests.
\[\begin{align*}
& P(\text{rejecting $H_0$ in at least one of the $m$ tests}\mid \text{all }H_0\text{'s are true})\\[2ex]
=& 1 - (1-\alpha_{\textrm{Bonf}})^m\\[2ex]
=& 1 - \left(1-\frac{\alpha}{m}\right)^m\leq \alpha
\end{align*}\] For \(\alpha = 0.05\) and \(m=20\colon\) \[\begin{align*}
1 - \left(1-\frac{0.05}{20}\right)^{20} &=
1 - \left(1-0.0025\right)^{20} = 0.049 < 0.05
\end{align*}\]


Alternatives to the Bonferroni correction:

Holm–Bonferroni method
Hochberg’s step-up procedure

✅ Correct Interpretation of the \(\textrm{p}\)-Value






🤓 Interpreting Small \(\textrm{p}\)-Values: \(\;\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} < \alpha\)

Decision Theory: When we reject \(H_0\) (because \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} < \alpha\)), we falsely reject a true \(H_0\) (type I error) with probability \(\alpha\). 👉 This is why we choose small significance levels such as \(\alpha = 0.05\) or \(\alpha = 0.01.\)

With a very large sample (\(n\) large) or low data variability (\(\operatorname{Var}(X)\) small), even tiny and unimportant effects will yield very small \(\mathrm{p}\)-values.


📢 A small \(\mathrm{p}\)-value signals statistical evidence — not necessarily practical importance.









⚠️ Interpreting Large \(\mathrm{p}\)-Values: \(\;\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} \geq \alpha\)





Consistency with \(H_0\): A large \(\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) means the observed test statistic \(\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) is consistent with the null hypothesis \(H_0\). ❗️However, this does not mean that \(H_0\) is true or confirmed.

Possible Reasons for Large \(\mathrm{p}\)-Values: Large \(\mathrm{p}\)-values (even \(\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} \approx 1\)) can occur when a real effect is simply too small to detect, for example if

the sample size \(n\) is small, or
the data variability \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\) is large.


Decision Theory: When we fail to reject \(H_0\) (because \(\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} \geq \alpha\)), we cannot conclude that \(H_0\) is true — only that we do not have enough evidence to reject it. We also do not know the probability of a type II error (falsely accepting \(H_0\)).


📢 Statistical tests are designed to reject \(H_0\) when evidence is strong — not to prove that \(H_0\) is true.

1.3 🤔 \(\mathrm{p}\)-Values: Misunderstood and Misused
\(\mathrm{p}\)-values can be powerful tools — when used correctly. But in practice, they’re often misinterpreted or misused, leading to a surprising amount of published “bad science.”
This misuse has sparked an ongoing debate: Should we rely on \(\mathrm{p}\)-values and the concept of statistical significance at all?
📚 Further reading:


The problem with p Values: How significant are they, really? (Cumming 2013)


Scientific method: Statistical errors (Nuzzo 2014)


Scientists rise up against statistical significance (Amrhein, Greenland, and McShane 2019)


To clarify what \(\mathrm{p}\)-values and statistical significance actually mean (and what they don’t), the American Statistical Association (ASA) published two landmark position papers:
📄 ASA Statements:


The ASA statement on p-values: Context, process, and purpose (Wasserstein and Lazar 2016)


Moving to a world beyond “p< 0.05” (Wasserstein, Schirm, and Lazar 2019)



1.3.1 🧭 What \(\mathrm{p}\)-Values Tell Us — and What They Don’t






✅ What \(\mathrm{p}\)-values do tell us





They measure how compatible the data (test statistic) are with the null hypothesis \(H_0\).
A small \(\mathrm{p}\)-value means the observed data would be unlikely if \(H_0\) were true.









🚫 What \(\mathrm{p}\)-values do not tell us





They do not give the probability that \(H_0\) is true or false.
They do not tell us whether a result is practically important.



📢 Key Message: Use \(\mathrm{p}\)-values as one piece of evidence, not the final verdict. Always combine them with effect sizes, confidence intervals, and context.

1.3.2 Correct Interpretation of the \(\textrm{p}\)-Value






🤓 Interpreting small \(\textrm{p}\)-values: \(\;\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} < \alpha\)





A small \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) suggests that the observed statistic \(|\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}|\) is inconsistent with the null hypothesis \(H_0\).
In that case, we may decide that \(H_0\) does not provide a plausible explanation for the data.
When we reject \(H_0\) (because \(\textrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} < \alpha\)), we accept a risk of falsely rejecting a true \(H_0\) (type I error) with probability \(\alpha\).
Therefore, choose a small \(\alpha\)-level!










⚠️ Interpreting Large \(\mathrm{p}\)-Values: \(\;\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} \geq \alpha\)





A large \(\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) means the observed test statistic \(\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{obs}}\) is compatible with the null hypothesis \(H_0\). ❗️But this does not mean that \(H_0\) is true or proven.

Even very large \(\mathrm{p}\)-values (e.g., \(\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} \approx 1\)) can occur when the deviation from \(H_0\) is too small to stand out from random variation — for example, if

the sample size \(n\) is small, or
the data have large variability \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\).


When we fail to reject \(H_0\) (because \(\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} \geq \alpha\)), we still cannot accept \(H_0\).We simply lack enough evidence to reject it — and we don’t know how likely we are to make a type II error (falsely accepting \(H_0\)).


📢 Statistical tests are built to falsify \(H_0\), not to verify it.




1.3.3 \(\mathrm{p}\)-Value Hacking
\(\mathrm{p}\)-hacking is arguably the most common misuse of \(\mathrm{p}\)-values. It happens when researchers keep adjusting their analysis until they find a statistically significant result \((\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{obs}} < \alpha)\) — even if there’s no real effect.
🧪 Typical tricks include:

Running lots of tests until one happens to be “significant.”
Changing the model setup (adding or removing variables) until an insignificant result turns “significant”.
Selectively including or excluding data points to turn an insignificant result turns “significant”.

This is called the multiple comparison problem — the more tests you run, the higher the chance of finding a false positive (falsely rejecting a correct \(H_0\)).

Multiple Comparison Problem






⚠️ Multiple Comparison Problem



 When multiple tests are conducted, the chance of finding at least one “significant” result purely by coincidence increases.
For instance, with \(m=20\) independent tests at the significance level \(\alpha = 0.05\), there is a \(64 \%\) chance of incorrectly rejecting at least one null hypothesis: \[\begin{align*}
& P(\text{rejecting at least one of the $m$ $H_0$'s}\mid \text{all }H_0\text{'s are true})\\[2ex]
=& 1-P(\text{not rejecting any of the $m$ $H_0$'s}\mid \text{all }H_0\text{'s are true})\\[2ex]
=& 1 - (1-\alpha)^m\\[2ex]
=& 1 - 0.95^{20} \;\approx \; 0.64
\end{align*}\]


Adjusting for Multiple Comparisons






🤓 The Bonferroni Correction



 The Bonferroni Correction requires using a more stringent significance threshold when multiple tests are performed; namely \[
\alpha_{\textrm{Bonf}}=\frac{\alpha}{m}
\] for \(m\) tests.
\[\begin{align*}
& P(\text{rejecting at least one of the $m$ $H_0$'s}\mid \text{all }H_0\text{'s are true})\\[2ex]
=& 1-P(\text{not rejecting any of the $m$ $H_0$'s}\mid \text{all }H_0\text{'s are true})\\[2ex]
=& 1 - (1-\alpha_{\textrm{Bonf}})^m\\[2ex]
=& 1 - \left(1-\frac{\alpha}{m}\right)^m\leq \alpha
\end{align*}\] For \(\alpha = 0.05\) and \(m=20\colon\) \[
1 - \left(1-\frac{0.05}{20}\right)^{20} = 0.0488
\]


Alternatives to the Bonferroni correction

Holm–Bonferroni method
Hochberg’s step-up procedure

📢 Key Message: Use \(\mathrm{p}\)-values as one piece of evidence, not the final verdict. Always combine them with

context.







Accept that there will always be uncertainty, and be thoughtful, open, and modest:






Be Thoughtful:

Know whether you’re doing an exploratory study (to generate hypotheses) or a more rigidly pre-planned study (to test hypotheses).
Invest time and care in sound data collection — good study design and careful execution matter more than fancy statistics.



Be Open:

Practice transparency — share your data, methods, and results so others can reproduce your findings.
Be honest in communication — “statistical significance” ≠ “scientific importance,” and one study alone rarely proves anything.



Be Modest:

Remember: there is no single ‘true’ model — every model is an approximation.
Stay humble about what statistical inference can (and cannot) tell us about the real world.
